Mission 1

Mission 1: Why do the French hide a charm in a January cake, and which traditions now divide them?

Make a guess: Why do the French hide a charm in a January cake, and which traditions now divide them?

Mission 1

The French calendar

  • France has 11 public holidays (les jours fériés).
  • Six are Christian in origin: Easter Monday, Ascension, Whit Monday, 15 August, 1 November (la Toussaint), Christmas. A secular Republic kept its Catholic calendar.
  • Others are civic: 1 May (la fête du Travail), 8 May and 11 November (end of the two World Wars), 14 July, 1 January.
  • 14 July (le 14 Juillet): national day by a law of 1880. It recalls the storming of the Bastille (1789) and the Fête de la Fédération (1790).
  • On the day: military parade on the Champs-Élysées, fireworks (le feu d'artifice), firefighters' dances (les bals des pompiers).
  • Watch out: un jour férié – a public holiday; faire le pont – to take the extra day off between a holiday and the weekend.
Mission 1

Customs through the year

  • January, Epiphany: la galette des rois. A small charm (la fève) is hidden inside; whoever finds it is king or queen and wears the paper crown.
  • 2 February, la Chandeleur: people make crêpes.
  • 1 April: le poisson d'avril – children stick paper fish on people's backs.
  • 1 May: people give lily of the valley (le muguet) for luck.
  • 21 June: la Fête de la musique (since 1982): free concerts in the streets.
  • 1 November: families put chrysanthemums on graves.
  • 24–25 December: le réveillon (late Christmas Eve meal), la bûche de Noël – the Yule log cake.
  • Your turn: "At Candlemas, we make pancakes."
    Show answer

    À la Chandeleur, on fait des crêpes.

Mission 1

Festivals across the French-speaking world

  • Québec: la Fête nationale du Québec on 24 June (la Saint-Jean-Baptiste); le Carnaval de Québec every winter since 1955, with its snowman mascot Bonhomme Carnaval.
  • Belgium: the Carnival of Binche – the Gilles dance in wax masks and throw oranges; recognized by UNESCO in 2003.
  • Switzerland: la fête de l'Escalade, Geneva (December), recalls the failed attack on the city in 1602; children smash a chocolate marmite.
  • Martinique and Guadeloupe: carnival ends on Ash Wednesday when Vaval, the carnival king figure, is burned.
  • Senegal: la Tabaski (Eid al-Adha): families gather, sacrifice and share a sheep, and wear new clothes.
Mission 1

The big cultural festivals

  • Le Festival de Cannes (since 1946, May): cinema; top prize la Palme d'or.
  • Le Festival d'Avignon (since 1947, July): theater; founded by Jean Vilar.
  • La Fête des Lumières (Lyon, around 8 December): in 1852 people lit candles in their windows; today light shows draw huge crowds.
  • Le Carnaval de Nice (February): parades of giant figures and la bataille de fleurs – the flower battle.
  • La Fête de la musique: created by the Ministry of Culture in 1982; copied in many countries.
  • Model: Ce qui me plaît dans la Fête de la musique, c'est qu'elle est gratuite et ouverte à tous.

Mission 1

When traditions meet laïcité

  • France's laïcité: the state is neutral toward religions.
  • Question: can a town hall display a Christmas crib (une crèche de Noël)?
  • Conseil d'État, 9 November 2016:
  • in a building housing a public authority (e.g. a town hall): not allowed, unless special circumstances give it a cultural, artistic or festive character (e.g. a local tradition);
  • in other public places (a street, a market): allowed in the Christmas period, if it does not promote a religion.
  • Some see cribs as heritage (le patrimoine, Provençal santons); others as a religious symbol that a neutral state should not display.
  • Watch out: la laïcité ≠ "laity"; it means the separation of religion and state.
Mission 1

Faut-il préserver toutes les traditions ? Argue both sides

  • Case: bullfighting (la corrida), legal only where there is an "unbroken local tradition" (parts of the south). A 2022 bill to ban it was withdrawn before it came to a vote.
  • Keep it (arguments supporters make):
  • La corrida fait partie de l'identité de certaines régions du Sud. – Bullfighting is part of the identity of some southern regions.
  • Elle fait vivre des villes entières pendant les ferias. – It supports whole towns during the ferias.
  • Ban it (arguments supporters make):
  • Une tradition ne justifie pas la souffrance d'un animal. – A tradition does not justify an animal's suffering.
  • Les traditions évoluent : on peut fêter une région sans mise à mort. – Traditions change: a region can celebrate without a killing.
  • Linkers: Au nom de la tradition, … · Pour les uns …, pour les autres … · Tout dépend de …
  • Your turn: "For some it is an art; for others it is cruelty."
    Show answer

    Pour les uns, c'est un art ; pour les autres, c'est de la cruauté.

Mission 1

Vocabulary bank and model sentences

  • une fête – a celebration, festival · un jour férié · une coutume – a custom · célébrer / fêter · un défilé – a parade · le feu d'artifice · un char – a float · se déguiser – to dress up · une tradition qui se perd – a dying tradition · le patrimoine immatériel – intangible heritage · la marchandisation – commercialization · transmettre – to hand down
  • Même si la pratique religieuse recule, beaucoup de fêtes religieuses restent des moments familiaux.
  • Si les fêtes locales disparaissaient, une partie de l'identité régionale disparaîtrait avec elles. (si + imperfect → conditional)
  • Ce qui rend une fête vivante, c'est qu'elle se transmet d'une génération à l'autre. (cleft for emphasis)
Mission 1

Exam tasks

  • Project Presentation angle: compare a celebration in a French-speaking community (e.g. la Tabaski in Senegal) with one in your community. Argumentative Essay prompt: Les traditions doivent-elles évoluer avec la société ?

Mission 2

Mission 2: French is spoken on five continents. Why, and what did the colonial past leave behind?

Make a guess: French is spoken on five continents. Why, and what did the colonial past leave behind?

Mission 2

The French-speaking world

  • About 396 million French speakers worldwide (OIF report, 2026), which ranks French as the world's fourth most spoken language.
  • About two thirds of them live in Africa.
  • French is an official language in 32 states and governments, e.g. Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Canada (with Québec), Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti.
  • la francophonie (small f) = all French speakers and places.
  • la Francophonie (capital F) = the institutions, above all the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF).
  • The word was coined by the geographer Onésime Reclus around 1880.
  • un(e) francophone · un pays francophone · la langue officielle · la langue maternelle
Mission 2

Why there? Two colonial empires

  • First empire (17th–18th centuries):
  • 1608: Champlain founds Québec (New France);
  • West Indies: Guadeloupe, Martinique, Saint-Domingue (today Haiti), economies built on slavery;
  • 1763: France loses most of New France to Britain.
  • Haiti wins independence in 1804 after a slave revolt.
  • Slavery in the French colonies: abolished 1794, restored 1802, abolished for good on 27 April 1848 (Victor Schœlcher).
  • Second empire (19th–20th centuries):
  • Algeria from 1830; West and Central Africa, Madagascar, Indochina; protectorates in Tunisia (1881) and Morocco (1912).
  • Belgium ruled the Congo, Rwanda and Burundi: one reason why the DR Congo is today the largest French-speaking country by population.
  • Not every French-speaking place is a former colony: Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg and Monaco are not.
Quick check
?Le Sénégal est membre de la Francophonie. What does the capital F tell you?
Mission 2

Decolonization, 1945–1962

  • 8 May 1945, Sétif (Algeria): demonstrations, then violent repression; thousands of Algerians killed (figures disputed).
  • 1946–1954: war in Indochina; defeat at Diên Biên Phu (7 May 1954); the Geneva Accords end French rule in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.
  • 1956: Morocco and Tunisia independent.
  • 1960: 14 territories under French rule in sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar become independent, e.g. Senegal, Mali, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon.
  • 1954–1962: Algerian War:
  • Évian Accords (18 March 1962); independence on 5 July 1962;
  • hundreds of thousands of French settlers (les pieds-noirs) leave for France;
  • many harkis (Algerians who served in the French army) are left behind, and many killed.
  • la décolonisation · l'indépendance · un colon – settler · la guerre d'Algérie
Mission 2

Who stayed French?

  • 1946: Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana and Réunion become départements (law championed by Aimé Césaire, poet and deputy for Martinique).
  • Mayotte became a département in 2011.
  • Today: five DROM (overseas departments and regions) and several overseas collectivities, e.g. French Polynesia.
  • New Caledonia: three referendums (2018, 2020, 2021) rejected independence; pro-independence parties boycotted the third. Serious unrest in 2024; an agreement on a new status (Bougival, July 2025) has not been put into the Constitution, and the question remains open.
  • Creole languages (e.g. in Guadeloupe, Martinique, Réunion, Haiti): most words come from French; the grammar is their own, shaped by African and other languages.
  • l'outre-mer · un territoire ultramarin · le créole · l'identité
Quick check
?Choose the best French for: "If France had granted independence earlier, the war could have been avoided."
Mission 2

The OIF

  • 20 March 1970, Niamey (Niger): founding of the agency that became the OIF; founders include Léopold Sédar Senghor (Senegal), Habib Bourguiba (Tunisia), Hamani Diori (Niger) and Norodom Sihanouk (Cambodia).
  • 20 March is the Journée internationale de la Francophonie.
  • 90 states and governments (2026): 53 members, 5 associate members, 32 observers. Some members are not French-speaking countries.
  • Secretary General: Louize Mushikiwabo (Rwanda), since 2019.
  • Aims: the French language, cultural diversity, education, democracy and human rights.
  • 2025: Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, ruled by military governments, left the OIF, calling it a political tool.
  • Summits: 2024 in France (Villers-Cotterêts and Paris); November 2026 in Phnom Penh (Cambodia), where members postponed the choice of the next Secretary General by a year.
Mission 2

Colonial legacies today

  • Language: French remains an official or widely used language in many former colonies; Rwanda moved its schools to English in 2008.
  • Money: the CFA franc is still used in 14 African countries; a 2019 reform ended the obligation for West African states to keep half their reserves in France.
  • Military: between 2022 and 2025 French troops left Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, Chad and Senegal.
  • Memory:
  • 2001: a French law recognizes the slave trade and slavery as a crime against humanity (loi Taubira);
  • 2005: a law asks schools to teach the "positive role" of the French presence overseas; after protests, that line is removed in 2006;
  • 2021: reports on Algeria (Benjamin Stora) and on Rwanda (Vincent Duclert);
  • 2021: France returns 26 royal treasures of Abomey to Benin.
Mission 2

Argue both sides

  • Should France apologize for colonization?
  • Arguments supporters make: Reconnaître les crimes du passé permet d'apaiser les mémoires. – Recognizing past crimes helps heal memories.
  • Arguments opponents make: On ne peut pas juger le passé avec les valeurs d'aujourd'hui ; il faut plutôt que les historiens travaillent. – We cannot judge the past by today's values; historians should do the work.
  • Is the Francophonie a shared space or a tool of influence?
  • La Francophonie permet à des pays très différents de défendre ensemble la diversité culturelle. – It lets very different countries defend cultural diversity together.
  • Pour certains, la Francophonie sert surtout l'influence de la France. – For some, it mainly serves France's influence.
  • Linkers: Selon ses partisans … · Ses détracteurs estiment que … · Tout dépend de …
Quick check
?Choose the best French for: "Algeria, whose independence was proclaimed in 1962, …"
Mission 2

Vocabulary, model sentences and exam tasks

  • la francophonie · un empire colonial · la colonisation · la décolonisation · l'esclavage – slavery · l'indépendance · l'outre-mer · le métissage – mixing of cultures · l'héritage – legacy · le devoir de mémoire – duty to remember · la repentance · la restitution · le rayonnement – influence, prestige
  • Le français, qui était la langue du colonisateur, est devenu une langue partagée par des millions d'Africains.
  • Bien que la colonisation soit terminée, ses conséquences se font encore sentir. (bien que + subjunctive)
  • Ce qui compte pour beaucoup d'Africains, c'est moins le passé que l'avenir de leur langue. (cleft)
  • Project Presentation angle: how French and a local language live side by side in one country (e.g. Senegal, Haiti). Argumentative Essay prompt: Faut-il qu'un pays reconnaisse officiellement les erreurs de son passé ?
Mission check

?Which sentence is accurate?

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • 11 public holidays; 14 July national day since 1880; customs: galette des rois, Chandeleur, muguet, Fête de la musique (1982).
  • Francophone festivals: Québec (24 June, winter carnival), Binche, l'Escalade, Antilles carnival, Tabaski.
  • Debates: cribs and laïcité (Conseil d'État 2016); bullfighting, tradition or cruelty.

Mission 2

  • About 396 million French speakers, two thirds in Africa; francophonie (people) vs Francophonie (OIF, 90 states and governments).
  • Two empires → decolonization (Indochina 1954, Africa 1960, Algeria 1962) → overseas départements since 1946.
  • Legacies: language, CFA franc, troops withdrawn 2022–25, memory laws (2001, 2005), reports and restitutions (2021).
